tags.name: Packing
tags.description: What to carry, and what not to.

posts.title: Packing for six days on foot
posts.excerpt: Your luggage travels ahead, so the day pack is all you carry. Here is what goes in ours, and what stays behind.
posts.content:
Every evening your suitcase is waiting at the inn. That changes everything about packing: the day pack only has to get you from breakfast to the bath.

What goes in

Rain shell, a warm layer, two litres of water, a small towel, a hat, and something to sit on. Our guides carry first aid, maps and the snacks.

What stays behind

Heavy cameras, a second pair of shoes, and the guidebook. The guide is the guidebook.

posts.title: The ferry that waits for the fishermen
posts.excerpt: On the smallest island on our route, the morning ferry leaves when the boats are in. Nobody minds.
posts.content:
There is a timetable on the pier, and everyone politely ignores it. The ferry leaves when the last fishing boat has tied up and its catch is on board.

A lesson in slowness

We built a whole day around that ferry. It is the best day of Island Hours, and the one walkers write to us about afterwards.

posts.title: A night at the Inn of the Seven Pines
posts.excerpt: Seven rooms, a cypress bath and a garden of moss. Why we have stayed here on every Kumano journey since the first.
posts.content:
The inn has been in the same family for four generations. The rooms open on to a moss garden, and dinner is whatever came out of the river and the hills that day.

The bath

A deep cypress tub, filled from a spring above the house. Go before dinner, when the garden is lit and nobody else is up.

posts.title: How to read a local train timetable
posts.excerpt: Two trains an hour becomes two trains a day surprisingly fast. A short guide to the rural lines we ride.
posts.content:
On the far north coast the line runs two cars and a driver who also sells the tickets. Miss the 10:42 and the next one is at 15:06.

Our rule

We never plan a connection tighter than forty minutes. The extra time usually becomes the best coffee of the day.

posts.title: Under the cedars, in the rain
posts.excerpt: Some of the finest days on the Kumano road are wet ones. Moss glows, the stone steps go quiet, and the forest smells of resin.
posts.content:
We walk in light rain. With a good shell and steady boots the cedar forest is at its most beautiful: mist between the trunks, water on every leaf.

When we do not

In heavy rain the guide changes the plan. A shrine museum, a long lunch, a train ride along the river. Nobody has ever complained.

posts.title: What our guides eat for lunch
posts.excerpt: Rice balls from the inn, a thermos of tea and a view. The simplest meal on the trail, and our favourite.
posts.content:
Every inn on our routes packs lunch for the next day: two rice balls, pickles, sometimes a piece of grilled fish wrapped in a leaf.

Where to eat it

Your guide knows a bench, a stone wall or a shrine step with a view for every lunch on every route.
